files.README.md:
Rainfall reporting - telemetry desk
==================================

The nightly export job and its notes live here. Start with
spec/export_notes.md for what the report contains and how the job is
launched.
files.nightly_export.py:
"""Nightly rainfall summary export.

Sweeps the ingest tree for reader-*.csv drops from the gauge network,
totals millimetres per station and writes the report to
out/nightly_summary.csv. The scheduler launches it from the project
root, so the sweep starts there and covers the whole tree.
"""
import csv
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
REPORT = ROOT / "out" / "nightly_summary.csv"


def collect():
    totals = {}
    for path in sorted(ROOT.rglob("reader-*.csv")):
        with path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
                station = row["station"]
                totals[station] = totals.get(station, 0) + int(row["mm"])
    return totals


def render(totals):
    lines = ["station,mm"]
    for station in sorted(totals):
        lines.append("%s,%d" % (station, totals[station]))
    lines.append("total,%d" % sum(totals.values()))
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"


def main():
    REPORT.write_text(render(collect()), encoding="utf-8")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

files.README.md:
Subscription archive report - membership desk
============================================

archive_rollup.py rebuilds the membership desk's monthly archive
report. It runs from the project root with

    python3 archive_rollup.py

and searches the whole project tree for the campaign folders'
events-*.csv exports. Campaign folders are named for the send that
produced them, not for when the events happened, and the exports sit at
different depths under archive/.

Every events-*.csv row:

    event_id,occurred,plan,amount_cents

    event_id       identity of one subscription event
    occurred       the day the event happened
    plan           plan the member took
    amount_cents   value of the event in cents

The archive report is grouped by the month in which an event happened -
the month of occurred - never by the campaign folder the export was
filed in. An event_id identifies one subscription event.

Date convention: occurred appears in three shapes, all meaning the same
thing - the day written first (DD-MM-YYYY, so 14-08-2026 is the 14th of
August 2026), an ISO date (YYYY/MM/DD), or an English month name
(Mon D YYYY, e.g. Jun 3 2026).

The report, written to standard output:

    month,amount_cents
    <YYYY-MM>,<amount_cents>   one line per month, ascending
    total,<amount_cents>

# Tuning deltastream in production: our checkpoint notes

*Posted 2025-11-20 by Marta Oyelowo · Cobalt Ferry Analytics engineering blog*

We run deltastream 1.9 in front of two Kafka sinks. After a month of load shaping, here is what worked.

## Start with the checkpoint cadence

Out of the box, deltastream's checkpoint_interval_secs is 120: up to two minutes of replay after a crash. For our 14k events/second feed that was too much, so we tightened it to 30 and watched CPU settle within an hour.

Backpressure was not our bottleneck; the sinks were. Raising sink concurrency did more than any ingest-side knob.

# Sizing and limits

This page explains how a bellwether node consumes memory, CPU, storage, and network, and how to work out what a deployment needs before it is asked to carry production traffic. It is written for operators who already have a cluster running and want to know which resource will run out first as flag sets and traffic grow. Every figure below is either a shipped default or a consequence of one that we have measured on the reference hardware described at the end of the page. Where a setting is described as shipped, the daemon uses that value when the key is absent from the configuration file, and the node reports the effective value through the admin endpoint at startup.

Bellwether is a read-heavy service. Almost all of the work a node does is evaluating flag rules against an SDK request, and almost none of it is writing. That asymmetry shapes every resource story on this page: memory is dominated by the compiled rule set, CPU is dominated by evaluation, storage is dominated by snapshots, and the network is dominated by the periodic exchange between nodes. If you are sizing a deployment for the first time, read the memory and evaluation sections first; the rest of the page assumes you have a working mental model of the two.

## Deployment shapes

There are three shapes we see in practice, and the sizing advice differs enough between them that it is worth naming them.

A **standard cluster** is three to seven nodes in one region, all serving SDK traffic, all holding the full rule set. It is the shape most teams start with and the one this page assumes unless stated otherwise. Every node can answer any request, so the cluster tolerates the loss of any single node without a client-visible error, provided the surviving nodes have headroom.

A **split deployment** separates writers from readers. One or two nodes accept flag changes and publish snapshots; the rest only read. This shape is common when flag administration is restricted to a change-management environment while SDK traffic comes from many networks. Readers hold the full rule set in memory just like a standard cluster; the only difference is that they never serve the admin interface.

An **edge deployment** pushes evaluation to many small nodes close to clients, with a central cluster for administration. Edge nodes usually hold a filtered subset of the rule set, chosen by project or by geography, because they cannot afford the memory of the full set. Filtering is a configuration decision, not an automatic one, and getting it wrong is the most common source of wildly wrong capacity estimates: operators size edge nodes for the filtered set and then wonder why the node reports a much larger working set than expected.

The rest of this page describes a single node. Multiply by the number of nodes only for storage and network; memory and CPU do not add up across nodes in any useful way because each node is an independent replica.

## Memory budgeting

Memory is the resource that surprises people. A bellwether node with a small flag set can run in a few tens of megabytes, while a node with a large one can want several gigabytes, and the growth is not linear in the number of flags. Four things consume memory, and they are worth separating because they grow at different rates.

### Per-flag-set overhead

Every flag set carries a fixed overhead before any rules are compiled: the set's metadata, its targeting keys, its segment definitions, and the index entries that let the evaluator skip sets that cannot match a request. On the reference hardware this overhead measures about eleven kilobytes per set, so ten thousand sets cost roughly one hundred megabytes before a single rule is compiled. Teams that model flags as one set per customer run into this first; teams that keep sets coarse rarely notice it.

The overhead is not linear in set count at the margins. As the set count grows, the index that maps targeting keys to sets grows with it, and the index is a sorted structure whose per-entry cost is higher than the metadata itself. We have measured a mild superlinear trend above roughly forty thousand sets, which is one reason the admin interface warns when a project crosses twenty thousand.

### Rule cache accounting

Compiled rules are the largest consumer of memory in most deployments. Each rule is compiled into a small evaluator object, and the compiled form is several times larger than the rule's source text. The expansion factor depends on the operators involved: a rule that tests a single string equality compiles to something compact, while a rule that combines several segment memberships, a numeric range, and a percentage rollout compiles to a considerably larger object with its own lookup tables.

The practical advice is to measure rather than to model. The admin interface reports the compiled rule count and an estimate of the compiled resident size, and the estimate is derived from the same accounting the node uses internally. If the number is larger than you expected, look for rules that repeat a segment membership many times; folding them into a named segment usually shrinks both the source and the compiled form.

### Snapshot residency

Each node holds the current snapshot and, for a short period after an update, the previous snapshot as well. Holding two snapshots during the overlap is deliberate: it lets in-flight evaluations finish against the snapshot they started with, which keeps a single evaluation internally consistent even while the rule set changes underneath it. The overlap period defaults to a small number of seconds and is bounded by the longest evaluation the node has observed recently, so it is normally invisible.

Snapshot residency becomes visible when snapshots are large and updates are frequent. A team that publishes a change every few seconds on a multi-gigabyte rule set will see memory oscillate as the two snapshots overlap. The fix is to batch changes rather than to shrink the rule set; the snapshot size is a function of the rules, and the overlap duration is a function of evaluation latency.

### Working set summary

Adding the four components gives the node's working set. The admin endpoint reports the working set directly, and it is the number to compare against the node's memory limit, not the size of the snapshot file on disk. A snapshot file is compressed and laid out for fast loading; the in-memory working set is neither, and it is routinely two to three times the file size.

## Evaluation throughput

Evaluation is where the CPU goes. A node spends the overwhelming majority of its CPU time in the evaluator, with the remainder split between snapshot loading during an update and the periodic background tasks described later on this page.

### Concurrency limits

The evaluator runs each request on a worker from a fixed pool, and the pool's size is bounded by one setting. The shipped default for max_concurrent_evaluations is 640 per node. The pool is sized for evaluation-bound work rather than for request count: an SDK request that asks about a single flag costs the same as one that asks about forty, because the evaluator walks the whole rule set for the request's target either way. Raising the limit above the default helps only when evaluations are short and the node has spare CPU; on a node that is already CPU-saturated it converts a clean queue into context-switch churn and makes tail latency worse.

The default is deliberately set above the point at which a reference node saturates, so that a healthy node never queues behind its own limit. Adjust it downward only on memory-constrained edge nodes, where each in-flight evaluation holds a reference to the snapshot and therefore delays the release of the previous one.

### Queueing and overflow

Requests beyond the limit wait in a queue. The queue is bounded, and a request that finds it full is rejected rather than allowed to wait indefinitely, because an SDK would rather receive a fast error and fall back to a cached value than block a user-visible code path. The rejection is counted separately from evaluation errors so that it can be alerted on without being confused with a bad rule.

Queue depth is the single most useful early-warning signal on an evaluation node. A shallow queue that drains quickly is normal under bursty traffic; a queue that stays deep for more than a few seconds means the node is past its comfortable operating point, and the right response is to add a node rather than to raise the concurrency limit.

### Backpressure signals

Two signals indicate that a node is under pressure. The first is queue depth, described above. The second is snapshot lag: the difference between the timestamp of the newest snapshot available cluster-wide and the timestamp the node is currently serving. A node that is busy evaluating falls behind on loading new snapshots, and a growing timestamp difference means flag changes are taking longer to reach clients than the freshness target allows.

Watch both together. Queue depth alone can be temporarily high during a deploy while snapshot lag stays flat, and snapshot lag alone can rise during a large rule change while the queue stays shallow. Only when the two rise together is the node genuinely short of capacity.

## Persistent storage

Each node keeps a local copy of the current snapshot on disk. The copy exists so that a restart does not require a network fetch, which shortens recovery and keeps a booting node from adding load to its peers.

### Snapshot cadence

Snapshots are written when the rule set changes, not on a fixed schedule. A node that sees no changes writes nothing. A node in a busy project may write a snapshot every few seconds, and the file is written to a temporary name and renamed into place so that a crash during a write cannot leave a half-written snapshot behind.

Storage sizing is therefore driven by change frequency, not by traffic. A quiet project needs almost no disk; a project that edits flags continuously needs enough headroom for two snapshots plus the temporary file, which is why the default storage reservation is generous relative to the snapshot size.

### Compaction

Old snapshots are removed as new ones are written, with a small retention window so that a node that fails to load the newest snapshot can fall back to the previous one. The retention window is counted in snapshots rather than in time, because the useful property is "the last known good one", not "the one from an hour ago".

Compaction runs in the background and is throttled so that it never competes with snapshot loading. On a node with very frequent changes the compaction work is a steady background cost; on a quiet node it is invisible.

## Network topology

Nodes exchange snapshots and health information over a gossip protocol. The protocol is designed so that a node needs to talk to only a handful of peers to hear about every change, and so that the loss of any peer does not partition the cluster.

### Peer synchronisation

When a node learns that a newer snapshot exists, it fetches the snapshot from a peer that already has it. Fetching is incremental: the requester and the provider exchange a summary of their index structures and transfer only the parts that differ. For a small change to a large rule set the transfer is a fraction of the snapshot size, which is why change frequency matters far less for network cost than the naive snapshot-size calculation suggests.

For a change that touches most of the rule set, such as a bulk import, the incremental path degenerates to a full transfer. These are worth scheduling outside peak hours, not because the network cannot carry them but because the receiving nodes have to compile and load the new snapshot, and that is a CPU cost that competes with evaluation.

### Gossip frequency

Health and version information is exchanged on a fixed interval, with a jitter added so that a cluster started at one time does not synchronise all of its gossip rounds. The interval is short enough that a change propagates through a seven-node cluster in well under a second and long enough that the background traffic is negligible next to snapshot transfers.

The gossip payload is small and fixed in size. It does not grow with the rule set, so a cluster with a very large rule set does not generate more gossip traffic than a small one; the difference shows up only in snapshot transfers.

## Observability

### Metrics that matter

The node exports a small set of metrics, and four of them are enough to run a deployment day to day. Working set answers "how close is this node to its memory limit". Queue depth answers "is evaluation keeping up". Snapshot lag answers "are flag changes reaching clients as fast as they should". Compilation time answers "how long did the last rule change take to become visible". Everything else is diagnostic.

It is worth learning the normal shape of these four on a healthy cluster before an incident, because all four have a diurnal pattern that is easy to mistake for a problem the first time you see it.

### Log volume

Logs are emitted at a moderate level by default. Per-evaluation logs are off unless explicitly enabled, because a node evaluating thousands of requests per second would generate an unmanageable volume and because the interesting signal is in the aggregates, not in individual evaluations. Admin actions and snapshot events are logged at a level that is on by default, and these are the lines to keep when shipping logs to a central store.

## Worked capacity example

Consider a standard three-node cluster serving a rule set of four thousand flags in eight hundred sets, with a request rate of nine thousand evaluations per second per node at peak.

Memory: the eight hundred sets cost roughly nine megabytes of fixed overhead. The compiled rules, measured with the admin estimate on the reference hardware, come to about seven hundred megabytes. Snapshot overlap adds a few percent during updates. A two-gigabyte memory limit leaves comfortable headroom, and it is the figure we would reserve.

CPU: at nine thousand evaluations per second, a reference node runs at roughly half of its evaluation capacity, which leaves room for one node to absorb another's traffic during a rolling restart. The concurrency limit does not need to change; the default already sits above the point at which this node would queue behind itself.

Storage: with changes published a few times an hour, the snapshot is small and infrequent, and a small disk reservation is ample. If the project moves to continuous publishing, revisit the reservation.

Network: the incremental snapshot transfers for small changes are negligible. A weekly bulk import is the only event that meaningfully exercises the network, and it is worth scheduling when the cluster is quiet.

Two additional nodes would double the evaluated capacity without changing any of the per-node figures, because memory and CPU do not add up across nodes. What changes is the failure budget: more nodes mean a larger population over which a single node's loss is absorbed.

## Segments and targeting

Segments are named collections of targeting predicates, and they exist to keep rules readable. A rule that says "user is in the beta segment" is easier to review than a rule that spells out six attribute comparisons, and because a segment is compiled once and referenced many times, using segments is also easier on memory than repeating the predicates inline.

Segment membership is evaluated lazily. When an evaluation reaches a rule that references a segment, the evaluator checks the segment against the request's attributes and memoises the result for the remainder of that evaluation. A request that touches the same segment from four different rules therefore pays for the membership test once. This is why a rule set built from a handful of well-chosen segments evaluates faster than one with the same logic inlined: the memoisation has more opportunities to help.

Segment definitions are part of the snapshot, so changing a segment republishes the rule set just as changing a rule does. A segment referenced by many rules is a wide change; a segment referenced by one rule is effectively local to it, and the incremental snapshot machinery transfers only the parts of the index that differ. Operators who care about change propagation time should watch how widely a segment is referenced, not only how many segments exist.

There is a limit to how deep segment references may nest. The evaluator expands references as it compiles, and a cycle in the reference graph is rejected at publish time with a clear error rather than at evaluation time. The depth limit exists to bound compilation memory; in practice, teams rarely exceed three levels, and a rule set that wants more is usually expressing something that would be clearer as a percentage rollout or as a separate flag.

## Percentage rollouts and consistency

A percentage rollout assigns a fraction of traffic to one variation by hashing a bucketing key, usually the user identifier, into a stable range and comparing the result against the rollout percentage. The property that matters is stability: the same user must land in the same bucket on every node and across every request, or the rollout will appear to flip as traffic is routed to different nodes.

Bellwether computes the bucket from the bucketing key and the flag key, not from the flag's numeric identifier and not from the node's identity. This means a flag keeps its bucket assignment if it is exported and reimported into another project, and it means every node computes the same answer without coordination. When a bucketing key is absent from a request, the evaluator falls back to the targeting key and reports the fallback so that it shows up in the metrics; a rollout with a high fallback rate is not really a percentage rollout at all.

Changing the rollout percentage does not reshuffle buckets for users who were already included. Increasing a rollout from five percent to ten percent adds users whose buckets sit between the two thresholds and leaves the original five percent untouched, which is the behaviour operators expect and the reason the bucket range is fixed rather than recomputed on each publish.

## Client SDK behaviour

Most of the evaluation cost a node sees is generated by SDKs, so their behaviour sets the ceiling on how economical a deployment can be. The two behaviours worth understanding are caching and polling.

Every SDK keeps an in-memory cache of evaluated flags, keyed by the request's targeting key and the flag key, and re-evaluates only when the underlying rule set changes. A service that asks about the same flag thousands of times per second with the same targeting key therefore generates one evaluation and thousands of cache hits. Deployments that report surprisingly high evaluation rates are almost always seeing one of two things: many distinct targeting keys, or a client that bypasses the cache by requesting a fresh evaluation on every call.

SDKs poll for snapshot updates on an interval with jitter. Polling is cheap because the exchange is incremental and the common case is "nothing changed", but the interval interacts with the freshness target. A short interval means flag changes reach clients quickly at the cost of more frequent, mostly empty exchanges; a long interval means fewer exchanges and slower propagation. The default interval is chosen to keep propagation well under the freshness target while making the empty-case exchange cheap enough to be invisible in the metrics.

An SDK that cannot reach any node at all falls back to its cached values and continues to serve traffic. This is deliberate: a bellwether outage should not become an outage of the services that depend on it. The fallback is reported by the SDK's own metrics, and a cluster that sees its client-reported fallback rate rise is usually seeing a network problem rather than an evaluation problem.

## Rolling restarts and upgrades

Nodes are stateless with respect to each other, and a restart costs one snapshot load. That makes rolling restarts straightforward, but the size of the rule set determines how disruptive a restart is to the node being restarted and, indirectly, to its peers.

When a node restarts, it loads the newest local snapshot from disk and then fetches anything newer from a peer. During the load the node is not serving evaluations, so a restart removes a share of the cluster's capacity for the duration of the load. On a large rule set this is measured in tens of seconds, which is why the standard procedure is to restart one node at a time and to confirm that the surviving nodes have absorbed the traffic before moving to the next.

Peers also feel a restart through the incremental fetch that follows it. The restarting node asks a peer for the difference between its local snapshot and the newest one; that peer serves the difference from memory, which is cheap, but the request is one more thing competing for evaluation CPU on a node that is already carrying extra traffic. On clusters that run close to capacity, operators sometimes restart during a quiet period for exactly this reason.

Upgrades follow the same procedure with one addition: the new binary must be able to read snapshots written by the old one. Snapshot format changes are announced in the release notes with the version at which the format last changed, and a node refuses to load a snapshot it cannot read rather than guessing, so a mixed-version cluster during a rolling upgrade is safe but may briefly run two rule sets. Keeping a rolling upgrade to a single minor version at a time avoids the case entirely.

## Common failure modes

Three failure modes account for most of the incidents we see in sizing reviews, and all three show up as a resource problem before they show up as an error.

The first is **unbounded flag set growth**. A team models one flag set per customer, set count passes forty thousand, and the fixed per-set overhead plus the growing index pushes the working set past the memory limit. The symptom is a node that is restarted by its supervisor during a publish and comes back only briefly. The fix is to collapse sets, and the admin interface's warning threshold is there to catch the trend before the restart.

The second is **a rule set that compiles much larger than expected**. A handful of rules that repeat a long chain of attribute comparisons can dominate the compiled working set even when they are a small share of the source. The symptom is a memory footprint that does not match the flag count. The fix is to move the repeated comparisons into a named segment, which also makes the rules easier to review.

The third is **queue depth mistaken for concurrency starvation**. An operator sees a deep evaluation queue, raises the concurrency limit, and finds that tail latency gets worse. The queue was deep because the node was short of CPU, and a higher concurrency limit simply gave the scheduler more work to interleave. The right response is to add capacity, and the queue-depth and snapshot-lag signals described earlier are the ones to read together before touching any limit.

Each of these is easier to diagnose from the four metrics than from logs, which is the main reason the metrics list on this page is short and stable.

## Choosing a memory limit

Set the node's memory limit from the measured working set, not from the snapshot file size and not from the flag count. The working set is reported directly by the admin endpoint, and the value it reports already includes the rule cache, the set metadata, and the snapshot overlap, so it is the number the supervisor's limit should be compared against.

Leave headroom for the overlap window and for the compiler. A publish compiles a new rule set in the background while the old one is still serving, so a node at its limit during a publish will be killed before the new snapshot is ready. A practical rule is to reserve a quarter of the limit above the steady-state working set; teams that publish rarely can get away with less, and teams that publish continuously should measure the peak rather than the average.

Memory limits that are too generous are less common than limits that are too tight, but they are not free. A node that is allowed far more memory than it needs will not fail fast when a rule set grows, and the growth will be discovered later, during a publish, when the node is least able to absorb it. Setting the limit close to the measured peak turns a slow surprise into an alert.

## Hardware notes

The measurements quoted above come from a node with eight physical cores, thirty-two gigabytes of memory, and a local NVMe device. Evaluation throughput scales roughly with physical core count up to the point where memory bandwidth becomes the constraint; beyond that, additional cores help less than the core count suggests. Memory latency matters more than memory bandwidth for evaluation, because the evaluator follows a pointer-heavy structure through the compiled rule set and spends much of its time waiting on cache misses.

Storage speed matters for restart time and for little else. A snapshot load from NVMe takes a fraction of the time it takes from a network volume, and that difference shows up directly in how long a node is out of service during a rolling restart. It does not affect steady-state evaluation at all, because evaluation reads from memory.

The network is the least demanding resource in a standard cluster. A gigabit link is ample for gossip and incremental snapshot transfers at typical change rates; deployments with frequent bulk imports are the ones worth giving more bandwidth, and they are also the ones worth scheduling differently rather than sizing around.

## What this page does not cover

Two topics belong to other pages. The rule language and its compilation rules are documented with the admin interface, and the details of snapshot format and incremental transfer are documented with the deployment guide. This page stays at the level of resources because that is the level at which sizing decisions are made.

If you are working through a sizing exercise and the numbers here do not match what your node reports, trust the node. The figures on this page are defaults and measurements on one hardware profile, and the admin endpoint reports what your deployment is actually doing. Use this page to understand why the node reports what it does, and use the node's own numbers to make the decision.

## Limits reference

The following table lists the shipped values of the settings most often adjusted, for reference when reading the rest of this page. Values are for a standard cluster node unless the description says otherwise.

| Setting | Shipped value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| max_concurrent_publishes | 512 | Admin publishes accepted at once; separate from evaluation. |
| evaluation_timeout_ms | 900 | A single evaluation that exceeds this is abandoned and counted as an error. |
| snapshot_retention_count | 3 | Snapshots kept on disk for fallback after a failed load. |
| gossip_interval_ms | 250 | Base interval for health and version exchange, before jitter. |
| compile_workers | 4 | Threads used to compile a new rule set in the background. |
| max_cached_flag_sets | 2048 | Sets held uncompressed in the compiled cache before paging. |

Settings not listed here are documented alongside the subsystem they belong to. The admin endpoint reports every effective value, including the ones this table omits, and it is the authoritative answer for a running node.

# Evaluation throughput on large flag sets

**halcyon-ops opened this thread on 2026-05-27**

We run three nodes and a rule set of about nine thousand flags. During a nightly batch job our evaluation rate roughly quadruples for twenty minutes, and one node starts showing steady queue growth while the others stay flat. Nothing in the configuration changed. Where should we look first?

**marrow replied on 2026-05-27**

Queue growth with flat CPU is usually memory bandwidth rather than worker starvation. Check the per-node working set against the node's memory limit before touching anything else; a node that is paging for its rule cache will queue while its CPU counters look calm.

**halcyon-ops replied on 2026-05-28**

Adding a fourth node fixed it. The nightly batch now spreads across four nodes and the queue stays shallow. We did not change any per-node setting, and the working set per node is unchanged.

# Thornfield in production: eighteen months of message routing

*Posted 2025-11-05 by Delphine Aveyard - Byteharbour engineering*

We put thornfield in front of every internal event stream in the spring of 2024 and have not looked back.

## What we run

Three broker clusters, one per region, all on 3.2.1. We pinned that release when consumer groups landed and have not needed to move since. The 3.2.1 tag has been stable for us in every region we operate.

## Routing

Topic per domain, one shared dead-letter topic, and a schema registry that rejects backwards-incompatible changes at publish time. Most of our operational pain came from routing policy, not from the broker.

## What we would change

Start with fewer topics than you think you need. We merged eleven into four last year and nothing broke.

*Delphine Aveyard leads event infrastructure at Byteharbour.*

# Thornfield quickstart on Kubernetes

*A hands-on walkthrough, last checked 2026-01-22.*

This walkthrough was written and tested against thornfield 4.0.0. Later 4.x releases keep the same manifests, so the steps carry over; check the release notes if you are on a different minor.

## Prerequisites

A cluster with at least three schedulable nodes and a default StorageClass. The examples assume `kubectl` is pointed at a scratch namespace.

## Deploy the broker

Apply the manifest and wait for the broker pod to report ready. One replica is enough for a walkthrough; production layouts use three.

## Send and read a message

Publish to the `orders.placed` topic and consume it back with the bundled CLI. If the consumer prints the payload, the broker is wired correctly.

## Clean up

Delete the namespace when you are done. The walkthrough leaves no cluster-scoped objects behind.
